title: GPU Egress Fencing and Service-Account Burst Control Playbook
author: Avery Chen
body:
Summary:
This playbook defines the design, IaC patterns, CI/CD requirements, alerting, and operational runbook for implementing egress fencing and service-account burst control for GPU tenant workloads. The goal is to prevent noisy-tenant egress spikes, reduce accidental cross-tenant DDoS risk, and provide predictable billing attribution while preserving controlled bursting behavior for latency-sensitive inference workloads.

Scope:
- Applies to all GPU tenant VPCs and shared-burst routing paths across cloud accounts where Redwood-managed inference services run.
- Includes Terraform modules, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy examples, NAT gateway/BGP patterns, CI/CD gates, monitoring dashboards, and incident runbook steps.
- Excludes edge/on-prem network appliances (see eng-private-deployments).

Objectives:
- Prevent >3x baseline egress spikes from a single tenant for more than 5 minutes without automated throttling/mitigation.
- Ensure egress-policy enforcement success >= 99.9% across all active GPU pools.
- Enable rapid isolation and rollback within 15 minutes for suspected egress leaks.
- Maintain billing accuracy for egress at per-tenant granularity.

Architecture Overview:
- Each tenant gets a per-tenant NAT pool/egress IP range (allocated via Terraform).
- Egress policy enforcement happens in three layers: Kubernetes NetworkPolicies + eBPF sidecars (per-node) for per-pod shaping + centralized egress-proxy cluster for policy-controlled burst gating.
- Smart burst tokens: short-lived service-account scoped tokens issued by the egress-proxy for controlled temporary increases above baseline. Tokens are rate-limited and audited.
- Fallback: If proxy is unavailable, flows are limited to baseline NAT throughput and flagged; critical inference routes can obtain emergency tokens via the canary fallback path (requires approval).

Key Components and Owners:
- infra-networking (owner): Terraform modules and BGP/NAT design.
- infra-runtime (owner): eBPF sidecar and egress-proxy code.
- eng-sre (oncall): Alerts, runbooks, and operational mitigation.
- cost-ops (billing): Billing tagging and export.

Terraform module example (minimal excerpt):
```
module "tenant_egress" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.internal/infra/terraform//modules/tenant-egress"
  tenant_id = var.tenant_id
  nat_ip_count = var.nat_ip_count
  egress_tag = "tenant:${var.tenant_id}:egress"
  enable_burst_proxy = true
}
```
Notes: module must be run with `terraform fmt` and `tflint` in CI. The module creates: per-tenant nat-gateway(s), tags, route-table associations, and a small proxy autoscaling group with IAM roles scoped to the tenant proxy.

Kubernetes network policy (example):
```
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-egress-through-proxy
  namespace: tenant-<TENANT>
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: inference-worker
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: <EGRESS_PROXY_CIDR>/32
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 3128
```
Operational controls and CI/CD requirements:
- CI pipeline for terraform module changes must include: `terraform validate`, `terraform fmt -check`, `tflint`, `checkov` security scan, and a `terratest` integration test that contrives a minimal tenant environment and asserts NAT IP allocation and tag propagation.
- egress-proxy changes: unit tests, integration test against a local eBPF shim, and an end-to-end staging validation that issues burst tokens. Canary rollout required.
- Gate: Any change that increases default tenant NAT throughput or adds unbounded egress IP ranges requires eng-sre approval.

Monitoring, Metrics and Alerts (recommended):
- Metrics to emit: `tenant.egress_bytes_total`, `tenant.egress_packets_total`, `tenant.egress_burst_tokens_issued`, `tenant.egress_denied_flows`.
- Dashboards: per-tenant time series with 1m/5m/1h rollups; heatmap of tenants by 5m egress rate.
- Alerts (PagerDuty -> eng-sre):
  - EgressSpikeHigh: tenant.egress_bytes_total (5m rate) > 10x historical 95th percentile for tenant, sustained 5m. Severity: P1.
  - EgressLeakDetected: tenant.egress_denied_flows > 1000 in 1m (indicates policy drift). Severity: P2.
  - BurstProxyUnavailable: healthcheck fail > 2m and >50% of tenant tokens failing issuance. Severity: P1.

Billing and Tagging:
- All NAT gateways and proxy ASGs MUST include `billing_tag = tenant:<TENANT_ID>` and `cost_center` tags. Cost-ops will run daily exports to match egress_bytes_total to cloud egress billing file. Discrepancies > 5% trigger billing-review workflow.

Operational Runbook (incident steps):
1) Triage: Identify tenant and scope using dashboard and `tenant.egress_bytes_total`. Record tenant_id and peak rate.
2) Temporary throttle: Scale egress-proxy to 0 replicas for the tenant's proxy ASG to force baseline NAT-only behavior OR apply per-tenant tc-scripts via the eBPF control plane to cap to baseline Mbps.
3) Preserve evidence: Capture `tcpdump` on affected node(s) for 5 minutes, and export proxy logs (S3 path: s3://redwood-ops/egress-incidents/<INCIDENT_ID>/).
4) If traffic is legitimate burst for latency-sensitive inference, issue emergency token via `egressctl issue-token --tenant <ID> --expires 15m` (requires two approvers if production).
5) Root cause analysis: Check recent deploys (CI job IDs), new container images, and tenant configuration changes.
6) Rollback path: If a tenant config change caused leak, revert via `terraform apply -target=module.tenant_egress` to previous module inputs and redeploy k8s networkpolicy.
7) Post-incident: Create incident page, schedule follow-up with tenant owner and cost-ops; update playbook if automation gap found.

Verification checklist (pre-rollout):
- [ ] Terraform plan shows only expected NAT IPs and tags.
- [ ] `terratest` passed with tenant allocation assertions.
- [ ] Staging egress proxy issued burst tokens successfully and metrics emitted.
- [ ] Alert rules deployed and tested against synthetic traffic.
- [ ] Billing export mapped to tenant tags for 7 consecutive days in staging.

Rollback and emergency mitigation patterns:
- Revoke burst tokens globally: `egressctl revoke-all --tenant <ID>` (immediate).
- If NAT-level leak persists, detach route to NAT and attach to isolated sink VPC (blackhole) while preserving logs.
- If proxy change introduced regression, revert canary via CI/CD `promote` pipeline which re-deploys previous image tag.

Testing and chaos experiments:
- Quarterly chaos test: simulate noisy tenant issuing steady 20% above burst budget for 15 minutes and verify automatic throttling and alerting. Document results in eng-infra/team-wiki.

Notes and FAQs:
Q: Why per-tenant NAT IPs instead of shared NAT?
A: Per-tenant NAT IPs enable precise billing, easier reputation isolation, and faster forensic traceability. Shared NATs reduce allocation pressure but make attribution and mitigation harder.

Q: Can tenants reserve longer burst windows?
A: Yes — through the billing-controlled reservation flow: tenant requests reservation -> cost-ops approves -> module updated with `preapproved_burst_token` TTL. All reservations are visible in the billing dashboard.

References and related policies:
- See `gpu-network-topology-and-tenant-isolation-patterns.json` for topology diagrams.
- See `gpu-tenant-credit-buckets-and-granular-throttling-policy.json` for burst budget math.

Appendix: example `egressctl` commands
- Issue token (normal): `egressctl issue-token --tenant t-123 --quota 100MB --ttl 300s`
- Revoke tokens: `egressctl revoke --tenant t-123 --token-id <id>`
- Snapshot metrics: `prometheus-query 'sum(rate(tenant_egress_bytes_total[1m])) by (tenant)' > /tmp/egress-snapshot.json`

Owner contacts:
- infra-networking Slack: #infra-networking
- eng-sre oncall: pagerduty schedule 'eng-sre/gpu-oncall'

If you plan to modify the Terraform module or egress-proxy, coordinate with infra-networking and eng-sre at least 3 business days before the change window.
